instances.brief: Puma workers each run `threads 12, 12`, so each process can hold 12 concurrent DB connections. The database pool size must equal the thread count so no thread queues waiting for a free connection. The current pool setting is too small for this thread count.
instances.teaches: Rails database pool size must equal the application server thread count. A pool smaller than the thread count means some threads will block waiting for a connection under load, producing `ActiveRecord::ConnectionTimeoutError` after the checkout_timeout expires.

given.content:
default: &default
  adapter: postgresql
  encoding: unicode
  host: <%= ENV['DB_HOST'] %>
  username: <%= ENV['DB_USER'] %>
  password: <%= ENV['DB_PASSWORD'] %>

# Puma config: workers 2, threads 12, 12
# Each thread holds one DB connection.
# Pool must equal the per-process thread count.
development:
  <<: *default
  database: app_development
  pool: 5
  timeout: 5000

wrong_outcomes.shows: 7 of 12 threads block on connection checkout at peak. After 5 s, `ActiveRecord::ConnectionTimeoutError` is raised and the request fails with HTTP 500.
wrong_outcomes.why_wrong: The pool is smaller than the thread count. Under load, threads that cannot immediately acquire a connection queue; after `checkout_timeout` (default 5 s) they raise an error instead of serving the request.

wrong_outcomes.shows: The pool setting was not the only thing changed. Every other line must remain byte-for-byte identical — changing the host or timeout alongside pool creates an untested config state.
wrong_outcomes.why_wrong: Only the pool value is under-provisioned. Editing any other line introduces a second unverified change that complicates rollback and root-cause analysis.

instances.reveal: The rule is: pool size = Puma thread count. With `threads 12, 12`, each process can run 12 concurrent requests, each requiring one DB connection. A pool of 5 means 7 threads always wait. Raising pool to 12 eliminates the wait entirely without over-allocating connections to the database server.

instances.brief: A scraper is hammering the `/api/` prefix. The current rate zone is misconfigured. Comment in the file states: legitimate clients peak at 12 r/s per IP. Apply the policy: cap at the next round number above 1.5 × legitimate peak.
instances.teaches: Rate-limit thresholds follow a two-step rule: multiply legitimate peak by the safety factor (here 1.5×), then round up to the next round number. 1.5 × 12 = 18, next round number above 18 is 20. Setting it below 20 drops real checkout traffic at peak; leaving it at 1000 r/s lets the scraper saturate the origin at 800 r/s.

wrong_outcomes.shows: Setting 10 r/s: peak checkout traffic (12 r/s) now triggers the limit, blocking 30% of real users with HTTP 429 at peak. Setting 1000 r/s: scraper sends 800 r/s through unthrottled, saturating the app tier and raising p95 to 1,400 ms.
wrong_outcomes.why_wrong: Any value below 20 r/s cuts legitimate traffic before scraper traffic. Any value above 20 r/s leaves the scraper partially or fully unthrottled — the point of rate limiting is to protect the origin, not just the client.

wrong_outcomes.shows: Changing `burst` or the `listen` port alongside the rate value creates two simultaneous config changes. If the burst value is wrong, it will be harder to tell which change caused the 429 storm.
wrong_outcomes.why_wrong: Only the `rate=` value needs correcting. The burst and nodelay settings are already correct for this zone. Changing more than one value at a time violates the principle of atomic config changes.

instances.reveal: The policy is: cap = next round number above (1.5 × legitimate peak). 1.5 × 12 r/s = 18 r/s. The next round number above 18 is 20. So `rate=20r/s` is the correct value. It gives legitimate clients a 67% headroom above their typical peak while throttling the scraper to a safe fraction of its attempted 800 r/s.

instances.brief: Cutover to a new IP is scheduled in 2 hours. The runbook requires: lower the A record TTL to 60 s at least one old-TTL window before the cutover, so resolvers will have expired the old answer before the IP changes. The IP address must NOT change in this edit — that happens in the next step.
instances.teaches: Pre-cutover TTL reduction works as follows: resolvers cache the old answer for up to the current TTL. Lowering the TTL now means that within one TTL window, all resolvers will re-query and pick up the new TTL. When the IP changes later, propagation completes in 60 s instead of 3600 s. Changing the IP in the same edit is wrong: the new host is not yet serving traffic.

given.content:
$ORIGIN example.com.
$TTL 3600
@   IN  SOA  ns1 hostmaster 2026092401 3600 900 604800 300
    IN  NS   ns1
    IN  NS   ns2
ns1 IN  A    198.51.100.1
ns2 IN  A    198.51.100.2
www 3600  IN  A  203.0.113.10
api 3600  IN  A  203.0.113.10
db  3600  IN  A  203.0.113.20
mail 3600  IN  MX  10 mail.example.com.

wrong_outcomes.shows: Leaving TTL at 3600: 62% of clients still resolve to the old IP 40 minutes after cutover because their resolvers cached the old answer. Changing the IP before the new host is ready: 100% of traffic immediately routes to a host not yet serving the application — the site goes dark.
wrong_outcomes.why_wrong: Pre-cutover TTL reduction must lower the TTL to 60 s without changing the IP. The IP change is a separate, later step. If the TTL stays high, propagation after the IP change will take up to one hour. If the IP changes prematurely, traffic hits an unready host.

wrong_outcomes.shows: Touching the `www` or `db` record alongside the `api` TTL introduces two simultaneous DNS changes. If the wrong record gets a low TTL, those records will be polled more aggressively during a window when the zone is in a transitional state.
wrong_outcomes.why_wrong: Only the `api` record needs its TTL changed before cutover. Editing any other record alongside it turns a targeted pre-cutover step into a zone-wide change, making the blast radius larger if something goes wrong.

instances.reveal: The pre-cutover sequence is: (1) lower the record TTL to 60 s while keeping the same IP, (2) wait one old-TTL window (3600 s = 1 hour) for all resolvers to expire the cached answer, (3) change the IP. Step 1 is this edit: `api 60  IN  A  203.0.113.10`. The TTL drops from 3600 to 60; the IP is unchanged. After one hour, every resolver will have re-queried and will hold the 60-second TTL, so the IP change in step 3 propagates globally within one minute.
